content: The minimum dataset for monitoring HIV, antenatal care (ANC), labor, postpartum, and follow-up of HIV-exposed infants is derived from several tools, including maternal health cards, ANC, labor and delivery, and postnatal care (PNC) registers, labor and postpartum records, and child health cards. An HIV-exposed infant register is essential for tracking the entire continuum of care, from birth to the final outcome of the exposed infant or young child. In some settings, a longitudinal mother–infant pair register can be used to document prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) interventions for mothers living with HIV and their exposed infants. This approach is particularly practical in settings with low HIV prevalence (<10%), concentrated epidemics, integrated maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH) and HIV services, or linked electronic information systems that enable longitudinal follow-up. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends organizing mother–infant pair registers by the expected date of delivery rather than the ANC registration date to facilitate tracking infant outcomes by birth cohort. Mothers on antiretroviral therapy (ART) should still be recorded in ART registers. Linking patient or unique identifier (UID) numbers for ART, ANC, and HIV-exposed infants across relevant monitoring tools can help ensure continuity of care. Key data elements for HIV care and treatment of pregnant and postpartum women and their infants include the age of the infant at additional HIV testing, the final HIV status of the infant (at 12 months in non-breastfeeding settings and 24 months in breastfeeding settings), the date of enrollment in HIV care, the infant’s UID, and the ART start date. Updates to these data elements have been made since the 2017 WHO guidelines. In 2020, updates to TB–HIV indicators included TB preventive treatment (TPT) initiation and completion, molecular diagnostic testing for TB among people living with HIV, and TB burden among new ART patients. New TPT regimens, such as 6H and shorter rifamycin-based regimens, were introduced. Additional indicators were recommended for high TB–HIV burden countries to monitor TB screening and diagnostic cascades. WHO emphasizes the need for integrated service delivery and patient monitoring to address the high comorbidity and mortality associated with HIV-related TB. WHO has introduced new tools for TB screening among people living with HIV, including chest X-rays, C-reactive protein tests, and molecular rapid diagnostics, in addition to the four-symptom screen. ART initiation within two weeks of starting TB treatment is recommended for all people living with HIV, regardless of CD4 count. National and global monitoring of TB/HIV collaborative activities is guided by WHO frameworks. HIV patient monitoring systems capture indicators such as ART initiation, intensified case-finding, TPT, and infection control. TB programs measure services to reduce the burden of HIV among TB patients, including co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT), HIV testing at TB diagnosis, and ART initiation for HIV-positive TB patients. Data reconciliation between ART and TB registers is necessary to ensure accurate reporting. Integrated patient records, either as separate HIV and TB cards within a single folder or a unified record, can simplify care and monitoring in high TB–HIV comorbidity settings. Electronic data systems, such as District Health Information Software (DHIS-2), and digital tools like the Prevent TB App, facilitate real-time data capture and cross-program collaboration. Differentiated service delivery (DSD) for HIV treatment is a person-centered approach that adapts services to meet the diverse needs of people living with HIV. It focuses on simplifying and decentralizing care, task-sharing, community delivery, and efficient resource use. DSD models are categorized into group models managed by healthcare workers, group models managed by clients, individual facility-based models, and individual non-facility-based models. Monitoring DSD implementation is critical to improving patient outcomes and program efficiency. WHO criteria for determining whether a person is established on ART include receiving ART for at least six months, absence of current illness (excluding well-controlled chronic conditions), good understanding of lifelong adherence, and evidence of treatment success, such as a suppressed viral load within the past six months. If viral load testing is unavailable, alternative indicators include CD4 cell count >200 cells/mm³, weight gain, absence of symptoms, and absence of concurrent infections. For further guidance on quality standards for differentiated ART service delivery, refer to the 2019 ICAP Quality Standards for Less-Intensive Differentiated ART Models.
